extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policymakers studying peer review; journal editors; funding-agency staff; scholars of science & technology studies
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how personal connections and review-process features influence reviewers' judgments of scientific manuscripts (retrospective manuscript review), and what mechanisms and policies affect bias. The page reports empirical analysis of PLOS ONE neuroscience reviews and discusses mechanisms, measurement, and mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate manuscripts only on scientific validity (PLOS ONE criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS ONE instructs reviewers to evaluate manuscripts’ scientific validity only, decoupling impact/novelty from technical assessment. (Also: manuscripts must be clearly written and adhere to the journal’s data policy.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the journal's explicit publication criterion: accept work meeting high standards of scientific validity regardless of perceived novelty or impact. The journal welcomes replications and negative results and provides a blank reviewer form. The authors exploit this criterion to isolate mechanisms of bias that are not driven by subjective impact judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review score scale (1.0=Reject, 4.0=Accept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews in the dataset use a 1.0–4.0 scale, where 1.0 = Reject and 4.0 = Accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study reports an observed favoritism effect of ~0.11 points per co-authorship proximity step on this scale. The scale is used as the primary dependent variable; inter-rater reliability for such scores is discussed elsewhere in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability as a metric of review consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-rater reliability (e.g., intra-class correlation, Cohen’s kappa) measures agreement among reviewers; typical ranges reported are about 0.10–0.40 across disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low inter-rater reliability (e.g., 0.19 reported for PLOS ONE in the study) indicates high disagreement even when reviewers are instructed to evaluate validity alone; used to argue that disagreement and bias persist even for technical criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nepotism / particularistic bias (connections, identity, affiliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularistic considerations—characteristics of creators irrelevant to content, including gender, race, religion, political ideology, and connections between creator and reviewer—are treated as sources of bias (nepotism is a key subtype).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical examples: reviewers favor applicants sharing institutional affiliation or prior co-authorship (e.g., friendship bonus ~0.22 points or 15% in cited studies). Nepotism is expected to be stronger in more competitive settings; typical mitigation is recusal of closest connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective review criteria (significance, novelty, originality, broader impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft evaluative criteria like 'significance', 'novelty', 'originality', 'broader impacts' are ambiguous and open to interpretive flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these criteria refer to uncertain future impact or are semantically ambiguous, they invite disagreement and favoritism—reviewers tend to interpret them in ways favoring work similar to their own. Recommendation: separating technical/objective vs subjective components may reduce bias from subjective criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools of thought as a mechanism for bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias driven by shared substantive scientific views—'schools of thought'—where communities holding similar theoretical/methodological assumptions favor work aligned with those views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism predicts favoritism that extends beyond immediate collaborators (e.g., co-authors of co-authors) because substantive views co-vary with social proximity. It suggests recusal of only closest ties may not remove bias; instead, diverse representation of schools is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal of closely connected reviewers (common policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy practice: recusing the most closely connected individuals (e.g., dissertation advisors or direct co-authors) from reviewing to mitigate nepotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness depends on the underlying mechanism: recusal may reduce nepotism but will not address bias from subjective criteria or schools of thought. The paper highlights that distant reviewers can also show favoritism, challenging the sufficiency of simple recusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection diversity (mitigation recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit reviewers embedded in diverse professional networks to reduce bias stemming from schools of thought and similar tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because substantive disagreement clusters with social networks, selecting reviewers from diverse scientific clusters is recommended over simply recusing closest connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition increases nepotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher competition for scarce rewards increases incentives for nepotistic behavior and favoring connected individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and theoretical literature cited suggests nepotism is more likely in competitive contexts (e.g., high-stakes grants); lowering competition (e.g., high acceptance rate journals) should reduce nepotism-related bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blindness of review (single-blind vs double-blind) as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blind review allows reviewers to see authors’ identities/affiliations; double-blind conceals them. Evidence on their impact on reducing relational bias is inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some trials show that successful blinding reduces favoritism, but other studies find small or no effects. Editors doubt moving to double-blind would necessarily improve outcomes; the paper does not rely on a single conclusion about blinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure personal connections by co-authorship distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalization: personal connections measured by minimum co-authorship distance in the co-authorship network (1 = co-author, 2 = co-author of co-author, 3 = co-author of co-author of co-author, 3+ recoded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study finds reviewers favor authors by ~0.11 points per step of proximity. Due to missing data and API limits, distances 4+ are recoded as 3 (reported as '3+'). The network is constructed 'one-level-out' from seed nodes (authors, reviewers, editors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct co-authorship network with bibliographic database (Scopus) and h-index matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Scopus author search API to match names to disambiguated profiles and to retrieve each scientist’s co-authors and h-index for covariates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats: Scopus does not index all outputs (e.g., conference proceedings), returns up to 179 co-authors per query (artifactual peak), and can include links created after the focal period, which can bias measured distances. Secondary edit-distance matching used when multiple results are returned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data privacy and ethical handling of sensitive review data
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect reviewer confidentiality by encrypting source data, removing identifiers, and adding noise (3% of decisions randomly flipped) before analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps were required by journal confidentiality agreements and IRB; they are explicit methodological constraints that affect analysis and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for measurement error in network distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing nodes/edges in the co-authorship network bias measured distances upward; co-authorship ties established after the focal date bias distances downward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 47.6% of measured relationships were >3, and due to Scopus API limits, the authors recode distances 4+ as 3. A random sample showed ~23% of recorded links did not exist in 2012, indicating a temporal measurement error that tends to decrease measured distances relative to the 2012 reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate methodological and non-methodological ratings when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewers rate methodological/technical aspects separately from subjective aspects, agreement on methodological aspects is not necessarily higher than on significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from prior studies shows methodological assessments can be as contested as subjective ones; the implication is that separating components may not fully remove disagreement, but clarity can help identify mechanism sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors’ suggested reviewers as a predictor of reviewer closeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors often nominate suggested reviewers; suggested status is correlated with co-authorship proximity and thus may predict reviewer favoritism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-authorship distances are strongly related to whom authors nominate as reviewers, suggesting formal co-authorship captures affinities between scientists. Suggested reviewer indicator is used as a control/variable in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLOS ONE contextual features that affect bias (high acceptance, online, no space limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS ONE's high acceptance rate (~70%), online-only format, lack of space limitations, and mission to publish valid science regardless of novelty reduce competitive incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features create a relatively uncompetitive environment that should lower nepotism but do not eliminate bias due to schools of thought or subjective interpretations of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial behaviors can introduce bias (recruiting by connected editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may use personal connections strategically (e.g., to recruit high-quality articles), and editorial affiliation with authors has been associated with increased citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (Laband & Piette) shows editors sharing institution with authors can influence outcomes; editorial selection practices are an additional source of potential bias beyond reviewer decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical expectation: homophily causes taste similarity to decline with distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Homophily implies that similar tastes and substantive views are more likely among proximate network members and should fall smoothly with social distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theoretical expectation underpins predictions about how subjective-criteria and school-of-thought biases vary with co-authorship distance and motivates analysis of distance gradients in scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to decouple objective vs subjective components of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Where subjective criteria drive disagreement, separate review into technical 'objective' components (validity) and softer 'subjective' components (significance/impact) to reduce conflation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PLOS ONE’s model of evaluating validity alone is discussed as a way to minimize bias from subjective criteria, though the study shows that even validity-only review can exhibit bias from schools of thought.
